newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Landsbergis party ahead in Lithuania vote.
newsitem.headline: Landsbergis party ahead in Lithuania vote.

text.p: The party of Lithuania's independence leader, Vytautas Landsbergis, took an early lead on Monday as results came in from the second round of parliamentary elections but was not expected to get an overall majority.

Preliminary results from 37 of the 65 seats in contention in the second round showed that Landsbergis' Homeland Union was leading in 20 of them. The party won 35 of parliament's 141 seats in the first round on October 20.
Landsbergis, a short and stocky former music professor who spearheaded Lithuania's drive for independence from the former Soviet Union, was bidding to seal his comeback to political power.
"I do not think that we will get an overall majority," he told Reuters as he waited for the results at his party's headquarters in central Vilnius.
Estimates for the Homeland Union's second round performance were ranging between 30 and 38 seats, party officials said.
It has already displaced the former communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), a sweet revenge for their sweeping victory against him in 1992 elections.

The Homeland Union is already committed to a coalition with the Christian Democrats, who won 11 seats in the first round and were ahead in four of the 37 second round seats, so the two together were likely to be able to form a coalition.

A Homeland Union-dominated government is expected to keep Lithuania on the path to European Union and NATO membership but some aspects of its economic policy, such as the unpegging of its currency from the dollar, have worried foreign investors.

A low turnout was taking some of the shine off Landsbergis' victory. Just 36.53 percent of the electorate had voted two hours before the polls closed, compared with 48.08 percent at the same stage in the first round on October 20.
The Homeland Union performance was in sharp contrast to that of the LDLP, which gained only 10 seats in the first round and was ahead in just two in the second, preliminary figures showed.

Landsbergis came to symbolise Lithuania's independence fight, but people showed in the 1992 elections that they were weary of the economic chaos that accompanied the break from Moscow and the in-fighting within his Sajudis independence movement.
They turned instead to the LDLP and its leader Algirdas Brazauskas, who had led an earlier break of Lithuania's communists from the all-powerful Soviet Communist Party.
